claim: Six freely hovering Anna's hummingbirds were studied using acoustic nearfield holography with a 2176 microphone array in vivo.
source: Hence, we studied six freely hovering Anna's hummingbirds, performing acoustic nearfield holography using a 2176 microphone array in vivo, while also directly measuring the 3D aerodynamic forces using a new aerodynamic force platform.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the experimental setup and sample size used in the study.

claim: 3D aerodynamic forces were directly measured using a new aerodynamic force platform.
source: Hence, we studied six freely hovering Anna's hummingbirds, performing acoustic nearfield holography using a 2176 microphone array in vivo, while also directly measuring the 3D aerodynamic forces using a new aerodynamic force platform.
evidence: The abstract describes the direct measurement of aerodynamic forces using a specialized platform.

claim: The timbre of the hummingbird's hum arises from the oscillating lift and drag forces on each wing.
source: We corroborate the acoustic measurements by developing an idealized acoustic model that integrates the aerodynamic forces with wing kinematics, which shows how the timbre of the hummingbird's hum arises from the oscillating lift and drag forces on each wing.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the acoustic model that integrates aerodynamic forces with wing kinematics.

claim: The characteristic humming timbre and radiated power of flapping wings originates from the higher harmonics in the aerodynamic forces that support bodyweight.
source: Comparing birds and insects, we find that the characteristic humming timbre and radiated power of their flapping wings originates from the higher harmonics in the aerodynamic forces that support their bodyweight.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a comparative finding across birds and insects.

claim: Allometric deviation makes larger birds quieter and elongated flies louder.
source: Our model analysis across insects and birds shows that allometric deviation makes larger birds quieter and elongated flies louder, while also clarifying complex bioacoustic behavior.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from model analysis across species.

claim: Male Drosophila use aerodynamically functional wings to create humming songs near their flapping frequency to increase female receptivity to mating.
source: Male Drosophila use aerodynamically functional wings to create humming songs near their flapping frequency to increase female receptivity to mating (von Schilcher, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to von Schilcher, 1976.

claim: Male and female mosquitoes duet at the third harmonic of their wingbeat frequency.
source: In a more sophisticated form of courtship behavior, male and female mosquitoes duet at the third harmonic (multiple) of their wingbeat frequency (Cator et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cator et al., 2009.

claim: Pigeons use modified primary feathers that sonate around 1 kHz when they start flapping their wings that incite flock members to fleeing and take-off behavior.
source: In contrast, pigeons use modified primary feathers that sonate around 1 kHz when they start flapping their wings that incite flock members to fleeing and take-off behavior (Davis, 1975; Hingee and Magrath, 2009; Niese and Tobalske, 2016; Murray et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Male broad-tailed hummingbirds generate a whistling sound with modified primary feathers in their flapping wings during displays to defend courting territories.
source: Hence, male broad-tailed hummingbirds generate a whistling sound with modified primary feathers in their flapping wings during displays to defend courting territories (Miller and Inouye, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller and Inouye, 1983.

claim: Silent fliers like owls suppress the aerodynamic sound generated by their wings to mitigate interference with their hearing and escape prey detection.
source: Silent fliers like owls, on the other hand, suppress the aerodynamic sound generated by their wings to mitigate interference with their hearing and escape prey detection (Geyer et al., 2013; Jaworski and Peake, 2020; Kroeger et al., 1972; Sarradj et al., 2011; Clark et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Owl flapping wings generate less structural noise because their feathers lack the noisy directional fastening mechanism that locks adjacent flight feathers during wing extension in other bird species.
source: Their flapping wings also generate less structural noise (Clark et al., 2020) because their feathers lack the noisy directional fastening mechanism that locks adjacent flight feathers during wing extension in other bird species (Matloff et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2020 and Matloff et al., 2020.

claim: Computational fluid dynamics simulations of flapping insect wings suggest that the acoustic field can be characterized as a dipole at the wingbeat frequency.
source: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of flapping insect wings suggest that the acoustic field can be characterized as a dipole at the wingbeat frequency (Bae and Moon, 2008; Geng et al., 2017; Seo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to CFD simulation studies.

claim: Flapping wing pitch reduction reduces the simulated nearfield sound pressure level.
source: Further, flapping wing pitch reduction (Nedunchezian et al., 2018) and increased wing flexibility (Nedunchezian et al., 2019) reduces the simulated nearfield sound pressure level.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nedunchezian et al., 2018.

claim: Increased wing flexibility reduces the simulated nearfield sound pressure level.
source: Further, flapping wing pitch reduction (Nedunchezian et al., 2018) and increased wing flexibility (Nedunchezian et al., 2019) reduces the simulated nearfield sound pressure level.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nedunchezian et al., 2019.

claim: Numerical simulation of the Ffowcs Williams and Hawkings aeroacoustic equation showed that the farfield hum of flapping mosquito wings is primarily driven by aerodynamic force fluctuation.
source: Indeed, numerical simulation of the Ffowcs Williams and Hawkings aeroacoustic equation (Williams and Hawkings, 1969) showed that the farfield hum of flapping mosquito wings is primarily driven by aerodynamic force fluctuation (Seo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Williams and Hawkings, 1969 and Seo et al., 2019.

claim: Hummingbird wing kinematics and unsteady aerodynamic forces are very repeatable during hover.
source: Hummingbirds are an ideal subject for developing and testing a model of flapping wing hum: their wing kinematics and unsteady aerodynamic forces are very repeatable during hover (Altshuler and Dudley, 2003; Tobalske et al., 2007; Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Earlier aeroacoustics studies of hummingbirds have resolved the farfield acoustic pressure field at a distance greater than 10 or more body lengths away from the hummingbird.
source: Earlier aeroacoustics studies of hummingbirds have resolved the farfield acoustic pressure field at a distance greater than 10 or more body lengths away from the hummingbird (Clark and Mistick, 2018a; Clark, 2008; Clark et al., 2016; Clark and Mistick, 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Wing hum can announce a hummingbird's presence, especially to the opposite sex.
source: Furthermore, wing hum can announce a hummingbird's presence, especially to the opposite sex (Hunter, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hunter, 2008.

claim: The hummingbird audiogram has yet to be established below 1 kHz.
source: Although their audiogram has yet to be established below 1 kHz (Pytte et al., 2004), this and other behavioral evidence suggests hummingbirds may be able to perceive the wing hum from a conspecific.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pytte et al., 2004.

claim: Behavioral evidence suggests hummingbirds may be able to perceive the wing hum from a conspecific.
source: Although their audiogram has yet to be established below 1 kHz (Pytte et al., 2004), this and other behavioral evidence suggests hummingbirds may be able to perceive the wing hum from a conspecific.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from behavioral evidence and citation.

claim: The aerodynamic force platform integrates both the steady and unsteady components of the pressure field around the bird up to three times the wingbeat frequency.
source: The aerodynamic force platform integrates both the steady and unsteady components of the pressure field around the bird up to three times the wingbeat frequency, which are associated with its net 3D aerodynamic forces.
evidence: This describes the technical capability of the measurement system.

claim: The microphone arrays measure the unsteady component of the pressure field around the bird up to ~1000 times the wingbeat frequency.
source: In contrast, the microphone arrays measure the unsteady component of the pressure field around the bird up to ~1000 times the wingbeat frequency (of which we studied the first ten harmonics): the acoustic field.
evidence: This describes the technical capability of the acoustic measurement system.

claim: The first ten harmonics of the acoustic field were studied.
source: In contrast, the microphone arrays measure the unsteady component of the pressure field around the bird up to ~1000 times the wingbeat frequency (of which we studied the first ten harmonics): the acoustic field.
evidence: This explicitly states the scope of the acoustic analysis.

claim: The oscillating lift trace consists primarily of the peak force generated during downstroke, which corresponds to a peak in its spectrum at the first wingbeat harmonic (44.2 ± 1.8 Hz).
source: The oscillating lift trace consists primarily of the peak force generated during downstroke, which corresponds to a peak in its spectrum at the first wingbeat harmonic (44.2 ± 1.8 Hz).
evidence: This is a direct measurement result from the aerodynamic force platform.

claim: The drag trace consists of two equivalent drag peaks during the upstroke and downstroke, which corresponds to a dominant peak in its spectrum at the second harmonic.
source: The drag trace consists of two equivalent drag peaks during the upstroke and downstroke, which corresponds to a dominant peak in its spectrum at the second harmonic.
evidence: This is a direct measurement result from the aerodynamic force platform.

claim: The 3D beak contact force on the artificial flower is negligible (5.2 ± 2.3% bodyweight).
source: We also measured the 3D beak contact force on the artificial flower from which the hummingbird was feeding, which is negligible (5.2 ± 2.3% bodyweight).
evidence: This is a direct measurement result.

claim: The acoustic radius agrees with wind turbine acoustics measurements at lower harmonics of the blade passing frequency.
source: This acoustic radius agrees with wind turbine acoustics measurements at lower harmonics of the blade passing frequency (Oerlemans et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oerlemans et al., 2001.

claim: The median difference between a single source model and a distributed model with 10 sources is 0.1 dB.
source: Indeed, we observe a median difference of 0.1 dB between a single source model and a distributed model with 10 sources (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a comparison result between two modeling approaches, shown in a figure.

claim: The model and recordings are in good agreement, because the difference in the magnitude of the sound pressure is ~4 dB or less for the first four harmonics.
source: The model and recordings are in good agreement, because the difference in the magnitude of the sound pressure is ~4 dB or less for the first four harmonics (maximum difference between the model and the measurement ±1 SD; Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and measurements.

claim: The first four harmonics represent most of the radiated harmonic power: ~99% of the simulated power and ~67% of the measured power for ±2.5 Hz bands around each wingbeat harmonic up to 180 Hz.
source: The first four harmonics represent most of the radiated harmonic power: ~99% of the simulated power and ~67% of the measured power for ±2.5 Hz bands around each wingbeat harmonic up to 180 Hz.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the power distribution across harmonics.

claim: The differences across all 10 harmonics may include some acoustic scattering by the wing and body, possible wingtip flutter and turbulent vortex dynamics contributions.
source: The differences across all 10 harmonics may include some acoustic scattering by the wing and body, possible wingtip flutter (Sane and Jacobson, 2006) and turbulent vortex dynamics contributions occurring multiple times during a wingbeat, so they overlap with the measured harmonics.
evidence: This is speculation about potential sources of differences between model and measurements, with one citation.

claim: The magnitude of effects combined is bounded by the differences in the measured and simulated spectra, which ranges from ~0.5 to ~7.0 dB.
source: The magnitude of these effects combined is bounded by the differences in the measured and simulated spectra (Figure 2A), which ranges from ~0.5 to ~7.0 dB (min. and max. difference ±1 SD; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between model and measurements.

claim: Odd harmonics are associated with a rotational pressure fluctuation mode while even harmonics are associated with a vertical pressure fluctuation mode.
source: The directivity of the acoustic pressure field varies between harmonics. Odd harmonics are associated with a rotational pressure fluctuation mode while even harmonics are associated with a vertical pressure fluctuation mode.
evidence: This is an observation from the acoustic field analysis.

claim: The 3D broadband pressure surface is roughly spherical in the nearfield and farfield.
source: Averaging directivity plots across all birds and flights, we find the 3D broadband pressure surface is roughly spherical in the nearfield and farfield (plotted in the middle of Figure 3B,C in black).
evidence: This is an observation from averaged directivity measurements.

claim: The principal axis is mostly vertical because the net aerodynamic force generated during hover opposes gravity.
source: The principal axis is mostly vertical because the net aerodynamic force generated during hover opposes gravity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of hovering flight.

claim: The orientation of the measured and predicted broadband holograms in the sagittal and coronal plane agrees within one standard deviation or less.
source: The orientation of the measured and predicted broadband holograms in the sagittal and coronal plane agrees within one standard deviation or less (Figure 3B,C; Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between measurements and model predictions.

claim: Both the near and farfield broadband directivity plots are pointed aft in the sagittal plane because the dominant first harmonic is oriented aft.
source: Both the near and farfield broadband directivity plots are pointed aft in the sagittal plane because the dominant first harmonic is oriented aft.
evidence: This is an inference from the directivity analysis.

claim: Higher harmonics contribute less to the broadband directivity, because their amplitude is much lower (<48 dB beyond the third harmonic).
source: Higher harmonics contribute less to the broadband directivity, because their amplitude is much lower (<48 dB beyond the third harmonic, Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on measured amplitude data.

claim: Due to the symmetry between the left and right wing, the coronal directivity points upwards at 90° across all measured and simulated harmonics.
source: Due to the symmetry between the left and right wing, the coronal directivity points upwards at 90° across all measured and simulated harmonics (Figure 3, Table 2), showing the hummingbirds performed symmetric hovering flight.
evidence: This is an observation from the directivity analysis that indicates symmetric flight.

claim: The first harmonic of the hummingbird hum is formed by an acoustic dipole, tilted aft in the coronal plane, which corresponds to the fluctuation of the net vertical and asymmetric horizontal force over a wingbeat.
source: In summary, the first harmonic of the hummingbird hum is formed by an acoustic dipole, tilted aft in the coronal plane, which corresponds to the fluctuation of the net vertical and asymmetric horizontal force over a wingbeat.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the directivity analysis.

claim: The second harmonic is formed by an upward pointing dipole, corresponding to the vertical force generation that occurs twice per wingbeat.
source: The second harmonic is formed by an upward pointing dipole, corresponding to the vertical force generation that occurs twice per wingbeat (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the directivity analysis.

claim: The third harmonic consists of a rotational mode like the first harmonic.
source: The third harmonic consists also of a rotational mode like the first harmonic (Figure 3H,I), as seen in the time-dependent 3D hologram (Video 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the directivity analysis and hologram visualization.

claim: The fourth harmonic consists of a vertical mode like the second harmonic.
source: Likewise, the fourth harmonic consists of a vertical mode like the second harmonic (Figure 3J,K; Video 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the directivity analysis and hologram visualization.

claim: Body mass and flapping frequency for hummingbirds, compact flies, elongated flies, and moths and butterflies were obtained from Greenewalt, 1962.
source: Body mass and flapping frequency for hummingbirds, compact flies, elongated flies, and moths and butterflies were obtained from Greenewalt, 1962, while the values for larger birds were obtained from Pennycuick, 1990; Figure 4E,F.
evidence: This describes the data sources for the comparative analysis.

claim: Values for larger birds were obtained from Pennycuick, 1990.
source: Body mass and flapping frequency for hummingbirds, compact flies, elongated flies, and moths and butterflies were obtained from Greenewalt, 1962, while the values for larger birds were obtained from Pennycuick, 1990; Figure 4E,F.
evidence: This describes the data sources for the comparative analysis.

claim: Radiated acoustic power scales allometrically with body mass except for compact flies and moths and butterflies, which scale isometrically.
source: Comparing the model simulation results with the isometric scaling relation we derived based on the model (Equations A25–50) shows that radiated acoustic power scales allometrically with body mass (Figure 4E) except for compact flies and moths and butterflies, which scale isometrically.
evidence: This is a finding from the scaling analysis comparing model predictions with derived scaling relations.

claim: The scaling law collapses the data well on average across species (average slope = 0.9; ideal slope = 1).
source: Considering flapping wing parameters are known to scale allometrically with body mass, we test the scaling law itself (Figure 4F), which collapses the data well on average across species (average slope = 0.9; ideal slope = 1), confirming the scaling law represents our model.
evidence: This is a quantitative validation of the scaling law.

claim: The low frequency content in the aerodynamic forces drives higher frequency harmonics in the acoustic spectrum of the wing hum.
source: Remarkably, the low frequency content in the aerodynamic forces also drives higher frequency harmonics in the acoustic spectrum of the wing hum.
evidence: This is a key finding from the model analysis.

claim: The higher harmonics originate from nonlinear frequency mixing in the aeroacoustic pressure equation between the frequency content in the wing's aerodynamic forces and kinematics.
source: The higher harmonics originate from nonlinear frequency mixing in the aeroacoustic pressure equation between the frequency content in the wing's aerodynamic forces and kinematics.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism generating higher harmonics.

claim: The predicted humming harmonics of the wingbeat frequency overlap with the measured acoustic spectrum.
source: The predicted humming harmonics of the wingbeat frequency overlap with the measured acoustic spectrum (averaged over all microphones).
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and measurements.

claim: The sound pressure level magnitudes of the first four harmonics match with a difference of 0.5–6.0 dB.
source: In addition to the good frequency match, the sound pressure level magnitudes of the first four harmonics match with a difference of 0.5–6.0 dB (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between model and measurements.

claim: This agreement is similar or better compared to more detailed aeroacoustic models of drone and wind turbine rotors.
source: This agreement is similar or better compared to more detailed aeroacoustic models of drone and wind turbine rotors, that predict noise due to blade-wake interactions and boundary layer turbulence (Oerlemans and Schepers, 2009; Zhang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with other modeling approaches, supported by citations.

claim: The regions of high and low pressure in the hologram are associated with wing stroke reversals.
source: The regions of high and low pressure in the hologram are associated with wing stroke reversals, similar to the pressure extrema observed at stroke reversal in computational fluid dynamics simulations of flapping insect wings (Geng et al., 2017; Seo et al., 2019; Nedunchezian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the hologram analysis, compared with CFD simulations via citations.

claim: Even though the input forces were lowpass filtered beyond the fourth harmonic, the amplitudes of higher harmonics are predicted.
source: Even though the input forces were lowpass filtered beyond the fourth harmonic, the amplitudes of higher harmonics are predicted.
evidence: This is an observation about the model's predictive capability.

claim: The acoustic model predicts hum harmonics that lie in an intermediate frequency range between the wingbeat frequency (~40 Hz) and the lower bound of feather sonations (typically >300 Hz).
source: Our acoustic model predicts hum harmonics that lie in an intermediate frequency range between the wingbeat frequency (~40 Hz) and the lower bound of feather sonations (typically >300 Hz; Clark et al., 2013a; Clark et al., 2013b).
evidence: This describes the frequency range of the model predictions, with citations for feather sonation frequencies.

claim: Small tonal peaks between the prominent harmonics are not radiated by the oscillating aerodynamic forces generated by the flapping wing, according to the hum model.
source: Indeed, we observe small tonal peaks between the prominent harmonics in Figure 2A that are not radiated by the oscillating aerodynamic forces generated by the flapping wing, according to our hum model.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing measurements with model predictions.

claim: These low amplitude peaks must radiate from another acoustic source such as aeroelastic feather flutter or vortex dynamics.
source: Consequently, these low amplitude peaks must radiate from another acoustic source such as aeroelastic feather flutter (Clark et al., 2011) or vortex dynamics (Ellington et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference about the source of non-harmonic peaks, with citations to potential mechanisms.

claim: For the hummingbird, the pairing of the first and second harmonics is due to the dominance of the pressure differential generated twice per wingbeat during the downstroke and upstroke.
source: For the hummingbird, the pairing of the first and second harmonics is due to the dominance of the pressure differential generated twice per wingbeat during the downstroke and upstroke.
evidence: This is an explanation of the observed harmonic pairing.

claim: The associated substantial weight support during the upstroke has been found across hummingbird species.
source: The associated substantial weight support during the upstroke (Figure 1B; Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018) has been found across hummingbird species (Ingersoll et al., 2018), which generalizes our findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies across multiple hummingbird species.

claim: The first four harmonics constitute most of the acoustic radiated power of the hum timbre.
source: In concert, the first four harmonics constitute most of the acoustic radiated power of the hum timbre—the distinct sound quality that differentiates sounds from distinct types of sources even at the same pitch and volume—which is determined by the number and relative prominence of the higher harmonics present in a continuous acoustic wave (Sethares, 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the harmonic analysis, with a citation defining timbre.

claim: Acoustic directivity is consistent from near to farfield, but changes based on the harmonic.
source: Acoustic directivity is consistent from near to farfield, but changes based on the harmonic.
evidence: This is an observation from the directivity analysis.

claim: The dipole structures are associated with the high vertical forces to offset weight.
source: In the 3D holograms, the dipole structures are associated with the high vertical forces to offset weight (Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hologram structures, with a citation.

claim: The dipoles measured for the first four hummingbird harmonics are strikingly similar to the ones found for hovering insects in computational fluid dynamics simulations.
source: The dipoles that we measured for the first four hummingbird harmonics (Figure 3D–K) are strikingly similar to the ones found for hovering insects in computational fluid dynamics simulations (Geng et al., 2017; Seo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with CFD simulations, supported by citations.

claim: Mosquito dipoles are oriented more horizontally because their wings generate unusually high drag at these harmonics due to their particularly shallow wingstroke.
source: Although the mosquito dipoles are oriented more horizontally, because their wings generate unusually high drag at these harmonics (Seo et al., 2019), due to their particularly shallow wingstroke (Bomphrey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explanation of mosquito dipole orientation, supported by citations.

claim: The sound magnitude that flapping wings produce depends heavily on the weight the flapping wings must support.
source: The sound magnitude that flapping wings produce depends heavily on the weight the flapping wings must support, and the timbre depends on the unique frequency content of each weight support profile (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparative model analysis.

claim: The fly and mosquito weight support profiles have the highest harmonic content and consistently radiate the most power when all else is equal.
source: Yet the fly and mosquito weight support profiles have the highest harmonic content (Figure 4B) and therefore, when all else is equal, consistently radiate the most power (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative model analysis.

claim: The parrotlet weight support profile has the lowest harmonic content and radiates the least power when all else is equal.
source: In contrast, the parrotlet weight support profile has the lowest harmonic content (Figure 4B); with most of the force being generated once per wingbeat during the downstroke, hence it radiates the least power when all else is equal (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative model analysis.

claim: For hummingbirds and hawkmoths, the proportion of weight support in upstroke versus downstroke is similar, giving them roughly similar vertical force profiles and similar acoustic power.
source: For hummingbirds and hawkmoths, the proportion of weight support in upstroke versus downstroke is similar (Geng et al., 2017; Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018); this gives them roughly similar vertical force profiles and leads to similar acoustic power (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a comparison based on cited force profiles.

claim: Flies and mosquitos may seem loud relative to their small size because while they have little mass, it is partially offset by the high harmonics in their weight support profiles.
source: This explains why flies and mosquitos may seem loud relative to their small size: while they have little mass, it is partially offset by the high harmonics in their weight support profiles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results explaining perceived loudness.

claim: It is the higher harmonics present in the weight support profile that directly affect the perceived quality of the sound—the timbre.
source: Furthermore, it is the higher harmonics present in the weight support profile that directly affect the perceived quality of the sound—the timbre.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the relationship between harmonics and timbre.

claim: Body mass is a strong predictor of radiated acoustic power because the aerodynamic forces needed to sustain slow hovering flight must be proportionally larger for heavier animals.
source: Body mass is a strong predictor of radiated acoustic power because the aerodynamic forces needed to sustain slow hovering flight must be proportionally larger for heavier animals (Weis-Fogh, 1973; Altshuler et al., 2010; Skandalis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by citations to flight mechanics literature.

claim: The associated increase in aerodynamic force amplitude drives acoustic pressure.
source: The associated increase in aerodynamic force amplitude drives acoustic pressure (Equation 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the acoustic model equation.

claim: Increasing flapping frequency increases the radiated acoustic power; flapping faster requires more power from the animal and injects more acoustic energy into the air.
source: Increasing flapping frequency also increases the radiated acoustic power; flapping faster requires more power from the animal and injects more acoustic energy into the air.
evidence: This is an explanation of the relationship between flapping frequency and acoustic power.

claim: Among the five groups, compact flies and moths and butterflies match the scaling law prediction, showing their acoustic power scales isometrically with body mass.
source: Among the five groups, compact flies and moths and butterflies do match the scaling law prediction, showing their acoustic power scales isometrically with body mass.
evidence: This is a finding from the scaling analysis.

claim: Other groups scale allometrically with either higher (elongated flies) or lower (hummingbirds and other birds) exponents of body mass.
source: The other groups scale allometrically with either higher, elongated flies, or lower, hummingbirds and other birds, exponents of body mass.
evidence: This is a finding from the scaling analysis.

claim: Allometric divergence can explain why larger hummingbirds are quieter, because they have disproportionally larger wings combined with an approximately constant wing velocity across an order of magnitude variation in body mass.
source: Allometric divergence can more readily explain why larger hummingbirds are quieter, because they have disproportionally larger wings combined with an approximately constant wing velocity across an order of magnitude variation in body mass, which is thought to maintain constant burst flight capacity (Skandalis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explanation of allometric scaling effects, supported by a citation.

claim: Large, elongated flies are unusually noisy for their body mass, with radiated acoustic power values well above the average scaling law.
source: Large, elongated flies are unusually noisy for their body mass, with radiated acoustic power values well above the average scaling law (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the scaling analysis.

claim: The disproportional noise generated by elongated flies is due to two combined effects: the higher harmonic content of their weight support profile and their consistent allometric acoustic power scaling.
source: The disproportional noise generated by elongated flies is due to two combined effects: the higher harmonic content of their weight support profile (Figure 4A,B) and their consistent allometric acoustic power scaling (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an explanation of the observed scaling behavior.

claim: The difference between the scaling exponents for mass is primarily due to allometric scaling of wingbeat frequency with body mass.
source: The difference between the scaling exponents for mass is primarily due to allometric scaling of wingbeat frequency with body mass because the simulated acoustic power scales with the right-hand side of scaling Equation 2 with an exponent of 0.9 (on average), close to 1 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an explanation of the scaling analysis results.

claim: Scaling Equation 2 is precise for birds, compact flies, and moths and butterflies.
source: Scaling Equation 2 is precise for birds, compact flies, and moths and butterflies, but the two other groups scale allometrically: larger birds get more silent (slope = 0.9) while elongated flies (1.1) get louder than predicted by isometric scaling incorporating the allometric body mass and wing frequency relationship.
evidence: This is a finding from testing the scaling equation.

claim: Larger birds get more silent (slope = 0.9) while elongated flies (1.1) get louder than predicted by isometric scaling.
source: Scaling Equation 2 is precise for birds, compact flies, and moths and butterflies, but the two other groups scale allometrically: larger birds get more silent (slope = 0.9) while elongated flies (1.1) get louder than predicted by isometric scaling incorporating the allometric body mass and wing frequency relationship.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the scaling analysis.

claim: The deviation may be partially explained by variation in wing stroke amplitude.
source: The deviation may be partially explained by variation in wing stroke amplitude (Bomphrey et al., 2017; Nudds et al., 2004; Azuma, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation about sources of deviation, supported by citations.

claim: Body size and wingspan in insects are highly variable amongst individuals of even the same species.
source: Further, body size and wingspan in insects are highly variable amongst individuals of even the same species (Debat et al., 2003), which may explain the larger variation.
evidence: This is an explanation for observed variation, supported by a citation.

claim: The predicted range over which wing hum can be perceived is approximately four meters or ~12 wing radii for rock pigeons.
source: The predicted range over which wing hum can be perceived is even larger in rock pigeons; approximately four meters or ~12 wing radii (Columba livia: flapping frequency 7 Hz, mass 400 g, wing length 32 cm; Pennycuick, 1968).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model, with cited pigeon parameters.

claim: The perception distance scales up with body mass.
source: The perception distance scales up with body mass (Figure 4E) and the auditory threshold of pigeons is exquisitely sensitive to the wingbeat frequency (Kreithen and Quine, 1979), which can thus potentially inform flocking behavior (Larsson, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the scaling analysis, supported by citations.

claim: The auditory threshold of pigeons is exquisitely sensitive to the wingbeat frequency.
source: The perception distance scales up with body mass (Figure 4E) and the auditory threshold of pigeons is exquisitely sensitive to the wingbeat frequency (Kreithen and Quine, 1979), which can thus potentially inform flocking behavior (Larsson, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kreithen and Quine, 1979.

claim: The low-frequency oscillating aerodynamic forces radiate high-frequency humming harmonics up to the tenth wingbeat harmonic and beyond, but the corresponding decibel amplitudes are insignificant compared to harmonics close to the wingbeat frequency.
source: Conversely, while the low-frequency oscillating aerodynamic forces also radiate high-frequency humming harmonics up to the tenth wingbeat harmonic (Figure 2A, Table 1) and beyond, the corresponding decibel amplitudes are insignificant compared to harmonics close to the wingbeat frequency (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an observation from the acoustic measurements and model.

claim: Some birds rely on specialized flight feathers that sonate loudly at high frequency to signal over longer distances how they are flapping their wings during flock takeoff, mating displays and displays to defend courting territories.
source: This helps explain why some birds rely on specialized flight feathers that sonate loudly at high frequency to signal over longer distances how they are flapping their wings during flock takeoff (Hingee and Magrath, 2009; Niese and Tobalske, 2016; Murray et al., 2017), mating displays (Clark et al., 2016) and displays to defend courting territories (Miller and Inouye, 1983).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Moths have been shown to respond to the wingbeat hum of birds in playback experiments.
source: Perception of wing whoosh also has implications for bird-insect predation, because moths have been shown to respond to the wingbeat hum of birds in playback experiments (Fournier et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fournier et al., 2013.

claim: An acoustic model analogous to the one presented has recently been used to simulate mosquito buzz in conjunction with computational fluid dynamics.
source: Finally, an acoustic model analogous to the one we present here has recently been used to simulate mosquito buzz (Seo et al., 2019) in conjunction with computational fluid dynamics to predict how aerodynamic forces (Bomphrey et al., 2017) color the mosquito's aerial courtship song (Cator et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to related work.

claim: When fruit flies use their wing as an aeroacoustic instrument during terrestrial courtship serenades, they reduce their stroke amplitude to a similar degree as mosquitos, which likely colors their timbre.
source: When fruit flies use their wing as an aeroacoustic instrument during terrestrial courtship serenades; however, they reduce their stroke amplitude to a similar degree (von Schilcher, 1976; Bennet-Clark and Ewing, 1968), which likely colors their timbre as in mosquitos (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited behavioral observations and model results.

claim: The 3D aerodynamic force platform flight arena consisted of a 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 m chamber, where each of the six sides is an instrumented carbon fiber force plate.
source: The 3D aerodynamic force platform flight arena consisted of a 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 m (height, width, depth) chamber, where each of the six sides is an instrumented carbon fiber force plate that mechanically integrates pressure and shear forces generated by the freely flying hummingbird (Ingersoll and Lentink, 2018; Lentink et al., 2015; Hightower et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus, with citations to previous work.

claim: Each plate is attached to three vee blocks, each instrumented by a Nano 43 6-axis force/torque sensor with 4000 Hz sampling rate.
source: Each plate is statically determined and attached to three vee blocks (VB-375-SM, Bal-tec), each instrumented by a Nano 43 6-axis force/torque sensor (4000 Hz sampling rate, lowpass filtered with an eighth order digital lowpass Butterworth filter at 180 Hz, silicon strain gage based, with SI-9–0.125 calibration, 2 mN resolution, ATI Industrial Automation).
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the measurement system.

claim: Wingbeat kinematics were recorded through three orthogonal acrylic access ports using stereo high-speed videography at 2000 Hz.
source: We recorded wingbeat kinematics through three orthogonal acrylic access ports using stereo high-speed videography at 2000 Hz using three pairs of DLT calibrated (Hedrick, 2008) cameras (four Phantom Micro M310s, one R-311, and one LC310; Vision Research).
evidence: This describes the kinematic measurement methodology.

claim: The kinematics were filtered with a fourth order digital lowpass Butterworth filter with a cutoff frequency of 400 Hz.
source: We filtered the kinematics with a fourth order digital lowpass Butterworth filter with a cutoff frequency of 400 Hz (~10 times the wingbeat frequency).
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: The acoustic setup consisted of a chamber that is 0.3 × 0.9 ×0.9 m.
source: The acoustic setup consisted of a chamber that is 0.3 × 0.9 ×0.9 m (height, width, depth).
evidence: This describes the acoustic experimental apparatus.

claim: The arrays surrounded the hummingbird with 2176 microphones (of which 25 ± 7 were disabled during each measurement).
source: Combined, the arrays surrounded the hummingbird with 2176 microphones (of which 25 ± 7 were disabled during each measurement; see Supplementary Information for details) while it freely hovered in front of a flower to feed.
evidence: This describes the acoustic measurement system configuration.

claim: The top and bottom arrays each consist of 1024 microelectromechanical (MEMS) microphones, while the two frontal arrays feature 64 microphones each with a sampling frequency of 46,875 Hz.
source: The top and bottom arrays (Sorama CAM1Ks) each consist of 1024 microelectromechanical (MEMS) microphones, while the two frontal arrays (Sorama CAM64s) feature 64 microphones each with a sampling frequency of 46,875 Hz.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the microphone arrays.

claim: The 3D pressure field was reconstructed from the planar array measurements using broadband nearfield acoustic holography (NAH).
source: The 3D pressure field was reconstructed from the planar array measurements using broadband nearfield acoustic holography (NAH).
evidence: This describes the acoustic reconstruction methodology.

claim: Each frequency component of the holograms was regularized independently using a Bayesian evidence method.
source: Each frequency component of the holograms was regularized independently using a Bayesian evidence method (Wijnings, 2015) before adding them all together to create the broadband NAH results.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology, with a citation.

claim: Linear predictive border padding was applied to the time signals to reduce distortions due to frequency leakage.
source: To reduce distortions due to frequency leakage, linear predictive border padding (Scholte, 2008; van Dalen et al., 2012) was applied to the time signals.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology, with citations.

claim: The radial directivity was computed using spherical NAH.
source: The radial directivity was computed using spherical NAH (Williams, 1999).
evidence: This describes the directivity analysis methodology, with a citation.
